abstract: |
  Middle Palaeolithic assemblages vary widely in technology, and whether this variability reflects separate cultural traditions or shared responses to environmental pressures remains a central question in the study of human evolution. Among the most distinctive of these technologies is Quina, a distinctive technological system built around thick, asymmetric blanks and prolonged tool resharpening, long interpreted as an adaptation to high mobility in open, seasonally structured environments. In Europe, Quina is mainly documented between MIS 4 and early MIS 3; in the eastern Old World it was, until recently, unknown. The identification of a complete Quina system at Longtan on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau changed this picture, but rested on a single case. Here we ask, first, whether the Quina-bearing surface assemblages of the surrounding basins share the technological concept documented at Longtan, and, second, how the entity they define was organised across the landscape. Analysing 166 Quina scrapers and 56 resharpening flakes from 27 surface localities across two basins, we find them statistically indistinguishable in technology from the excavated Longtan material: Longtan represents one expression of a broader regional practice, which we term the Quina Valley. Its raw material economy rests on a strong preference for trachyte, selected against local abundance for its cobble size and predictable fracture, and its technology shows no systematic variation across the landscape. Its setting, a dry-hot valley on the plateau margin, differs fundamentally from the glacial landscapes of European Quina, yet presents an ecological challenge of the same structure: patchy, seasonally organised resources requiring movement through heterogeneous terrain. This study identifies the first regional Quina entity in the eastern Old World and provides an ecological framework for understanding its emergence. Future excavation will be essential for establishing its chronology, identifying associated populations, and reconstructing the subsistence strategies it supported.

# Highlights {.unnumbered}

- First regional Quina retouch identified in East Asia; Longtan was not isolated.

- 27 surface localities yield Quina scrapers statistically indistinguishable from Longtan finds.

- Strong trachyte preference reflects cobble size and knapping quality rather than local abundance.

- Quina scraper remained spatially consistent across the landscape.

- Shared resource structures despite environment differences explain technological behaviour convergence.

# Introduction

In a period whose lithic variability has been read in turn as cultural tradition, site activity, change through time, raw material and degree of reduction [@bordesMousterianCulturesFrance1961; @bordes1950; @binfordbinford1966; @mellars1969; @geneste1985; @kuhn1995; @dibble1987interpretation], whether East Asia has a Middle Palaeolithic at all has long been contested. On the conventional view, substantial innovation in lithic technology was deferred until the Upper Palaeolithic, leaving no phase corresponding to the western Middle Palaeolithic [@gaoPaleolithicCulturesChina2013; @norton2009eastasian]. Recent discoveries have provided new evidence that is reshaping this long-standing understanding. Discoid technology is documented at Lingjing (\~125–90 ka) [@liTechnologicalBehaviorEarly2019], and Levallois technology at Guanyindong (\~170–80 ka) [@huLateMiddlePleistocene2019] and Jinsitai (\~47–37 ka) [@liEasternmostMiddlePaleolithic2018]. These finds indicate that the technological scenario of the East Asian Middle Palaeolithic is more complex than the conventional view allows.

The technology at issue here is defined not by a tool type but by a techno-economic system, the Quina system: thick flakes of markedly asymmetric cross-section, carrying a sharp edge on one margin and a thick back opposite; a working edge sustained through cyclical Quina retouch rather than merely produced; and the ramified reuse of the products of that maintenance, so that stone already in hand yielded fresh working edges as tools wore out. In the strict sense the system is documented in western and southern Europe within a narrow interval between MIS 4 and early MIS 3, whereas Quina retouch taken alone is far more widely distributed, reaching back in the Levant as far as MIS 11; the distinction between the two, and the criteria on which each is recognised, are set out in Section 2. Neither the system nor Quina retouch, however, had been securely documented in the East Asia. It is against this background that we identified a complete Quina system at Longtan, dated to \~60–50 ka [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a], the first Quina site in East Asia to be unambiguously characterised, formally excavated, securely dated and systematically analysed. This discovery not only filled a long-standing gap in the eastern Old World distribution of Quina technology, but also provided new evidence for reassessing the diversity and complexity of the East Asian Middle Palaeolithic.

More importantly, Longtan is unlikely to be an isolated case. Surface collections bearing Quina features have been recovered from river terraces at a number of localities in the Huangping Basin, where Longtan is situated, and in the neighbouring Binchuan Basin [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a; @xiao2024survey]. These finds suggest that Quina technology on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau may not be confined to a single site, but may instead represent a regional technological phenomenon of some spatial extent. The two basins lie in the Hengduan Mountains, in what is today the dry-hot valley zone of the Jinsha River drainage, under a monsoon-governed climatic regime unlike the mid-latitude, glacial-stage settings of western Europe in which the European Quina is documented; whether the two settings nonetheless resemble one another in the respects that bear on how technology was organised is a question we return to once the technological results are in place. All of the localities so far identified, moreover, apart from Longtan itself, are surface collections without absolute dates, so that whether they constitute a coherent regional technological entity is equally open.

The analysis proceeds in two steps. We ask, first, whether the Quina-bearing surface assemblages share the technological concept documented at Longtan, indistinguishable from the excavated material on the attributes that define the system while remaining distinct from other retouched tools, and therefore constitute a single regional technological entity. To answer this we systematically analyse the most diagnostic elements of the Quina system, the Quina scrapers and the resharpening flakes removed in maintaining them. If they do, we ask, second, how that entity was organised across the landscape: what stone was selected against what was available, and whether the technology varies with position in the landscape. Why such an organisation arose, and what its resemblance to the European Quina implies, the surface record cannot test; we take these questions up in the Discussion.

This study identifies the first regional-scale Quina entity in East Asia, which we term the Quina Valley, characterises its raw material economy and landscape organisation, and proposes on that basis a hypothesis of convergence grounded in the structure of resources rather than in any resemblance of climate. Sections 2 and 3 supply the background, the Quina system and the regional setting respectively; the first question is taken up in Section 5.1, the second in Section 5.2.

# The Quina system

The Quina Mousterian is one of the best-defined Middle Palaeolithic techno-complexes [@delagnes2006; @faivre2017], and what distinguishes it is not a tool type but a techno-economic system, the Quina system, whose defining features form three interlocking dimensions [@delpiano2022; @peresani2023]. The first dimension is blank production. Quina cores receive little preparation and are reduced through alternating, concatenated removals on sub-parallel and secant surfaces, with invasive detachments that optimise the volume of stone converted into blanks [@turq1989; @turq2000; @Bourguignon1997]. The target product is a thick flake, asymmetric in cross-section, with a sharp cutting edge on one margin and a thick, often cortical, back opposite [@turq1992; @hiscock2009]. This asymmetry is what allows such a tool to be repeatedly resharpened [@turq1992; @hiscock2009]. The second dimension is edge maintenance, achieved through Quina retouch. Here the working edge is not merely produced but sustained, and resharpening follows a regular rhythm [@lemoriniScrapersLifeHistory2016; @Bourguignon1997]. Early episodes detach relatively large resharpening flakes and leave convex scars, giving a plano-convex edge and preserving volume for later work; as retouch proceeds it concentrates on the margin itself, producing smaller concave scars with stepped or hinged terminations and a plano-concave edge that keeps the tool serviceable. Each generation of retouch therefore restores a working edge without drawing on new raw material. The third dimension is ramification of the reduction sequence [@bourguignon2004ramification; @faivre2017]. Resharpening flakes detached during edge maintenance carry cutting edges of their own and can be used directly, as use-wear analysis has shown [@claud2012]; in some cases they were themselves retouched into tools [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a]. Quina flakes, besides being shaped into Quina scrapers, are thick enough to serve as cores for small flakes (i.e. core-on-flake) [@hiscock2009]. Use-wear on scrapers and resharpening flakes from the same assemblages indicates that the two were put to different tasks, scraping and cutting respectively [@delpiano2022], so that ramification widened the functional range of the toolkit as well as extending its life. Efficient blank production, intensive edge maintenance and ramification together create an economy of stone use in which the thick Quina flake functions as a transportable and highly extendable package of raw material, yielding a large amount of working edge from a small initial investment [@hiscock2009; @delpiano2022].

The distinction between the Quina system and Quina retouch alone matters when its distribution is assessed. In the strict sense, with blank production, edge maintenance and ramification operating together, Quina system is documented in western and southern Europe within a narrow interval between MIS 4 and early MIS 3, coinciding with pronounced global climatic instability [@delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011; @delpiano2022; @frouinDatingMiddlePaleolithic2017].

Quina retouch taken on its own is far more widely distributed: in the Levant it has been reported in Acheulo–Yabrudian industries dating from as early as MIS 11 [@agamInterpretingQuinaDemiQuina2020; @FALGUERES2022101266; @zaidnerEndLowerPaleolithic2016]. The occurrence of so distinctive a way of maintaining a working edge in contexts this widely separated in time and space raises the possibility that Quina retouch is a recurrent solution to a recurrent problem rather than the signature of a single tradition.

# Regional geological setting and raw material sources

The tectonic framework of the study area determines both where its intermontane basins lie and where knappable stone is available within them. The area falls within the Jinsha River drainage in the southern Hengduan Mountains, on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau, and is controlled by a system of approximately north–south trending faults: continued relative uplift of massifs such as Yulong Mountains and Diancang Shan, alternating with subsidence of the ground between them, has produced a series of north–south trending intermontane basins, among them Lijiang, Heqing and Dali [@liJGS2023]. This alternation of uplifted ranges and downfaulted basins shelters the deeply incised valley floors from precipitation carried by the Indian monsoon and the warm, moist airflow from the southwest, and gives them, today, a dry-hot valley climate: descending air masses are adiabatically warmed by the foehn effect and the deeply incised floors lie in the rain shadow of the flanking ranges, producing a sharp division between wet and dry seasons and high insolation [@zhu2024; @yangReviewResearchVegetation2016]. The Quina localities discussed here are concentrated in two of these basins, the Huangping Basin in the southwest of Heqing County and the neighbouring Binchuan Basin, each of them cut by tributaries of the Jinsha River: the Caifeng River in the Huangping Basin, and the Sangyuan River together with its tributary the Liandong River in the Binchuan Basin (@fig-study-area).

![Study area, site/locality distribution, and geomorphological setting. (A) Location of the study area at the global scale and an oblique block three-dimensional terrain model of the study area. (B) Plan-view map of the study area. The white dashed line crossing the sites/localities indicates the profile transect shown in (C). (C) Topographic profile of the study area. Topographic data were derived from the Digital Elevation Model of the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM), with a spatial resolution of 30 m.](../figures/study_area.png){#fig-study-area width="5.9in"}

The two basins differ in bedrock (@fig-geology). Permian volcanic rocks are extensively exposed along the western side of the Huangping Basin, with Triassic sedimentary rocks predominating to the east, whereas the Binchuan Basin is largely mantled by unconsolidated Quaternary sediments and exposes its Permian volcanic basement only locally [@yunnangeology1973]. The volcanic sequence comprises basalt, tuff and trachyte. Because the rivers of both basins cut across these outcrops, volcanic cobbles were carried into the gravel bars of the valley floors, and it was these bars, rather than the outcrops themselves, that supplied the stone used at the localities.

![Bedrock geology of the study area, and the gravel bars that supplied its raw material. (A) Geological units of the Huangping and Binchuan basins on shaded relief, with the Quina localities in black and the five gravel-bar sampling points in red. The units were traced from the 1:200,000 regional geological sheet compiled in 1973 by the First Regional Geological Survey Team of the Yunnan Geological Bureau; their boundaries are generalised from that sheet and are given as context rather than as surveyed contacts. Relief is rendered from the SRTM DEM. (B) to (E) The surveyed gravel bars at sampling points 2 to 5, with trachyte and sandstone cobbles indicated.](../figures/geology_map.png){#fig-geology width="5.9in"}

At Longtan, optically stimulated luminescence (OSL) dating places the *in situ* cultural layer at \~60–50 ka [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a]. Taken together, the regional and local records, presented in the Discussion where they bear on the question of convergence, indicate that hominins were present in this landscape while the vegetation was opening locally, and across the MIS 4/MIS 3 boundary, as regional aridity gave way to a strengthening monsoon.

# Materials and methods

## Survey and selection of localities

The surface material analysed here was recovered during four seasons of pedestrian survey in the Huangping and Binchuan basins, carried out in 2010, 2013, 2016 and 2022. Survey followed the main valleys of the two basins, the Caifeng River in the Huangping Basin and the Sangyuan River together with its tributary the Liandong River in the Binchuan Basin, and each flight of river terraces was walked in turn. Survey areas and walking routes were designed to cover the full range of landforms that humans might have used in the past. Routes were recorded continuously using the mobile GPS application 2bulu, localities and artefacts were photographed, and a field form was completed for each locality giving its position, its place within the terrace sequence, its straight-line distance to the river channel, and the number and types of artefacts present.

Because this study is concerned with Quina technology, the localities recorded during survey were then screened, and only those yielding diagnostic Quina scrapers and resharpening flakes were retained. On this criterion, 22 of the 33 localities recorded in the Binchuan Basin and all five of those recorded in the Huangping Basin contain Quina specimens (@tbl-localities). Two consequences of this design should be stated at the outset. First, the criterion is one of presence rather than of degree: localities were retained on whether Quina pieces occur at them, not on how those pieces were made or how far they had been reduced, so that none of the technological variables analysed below entered the selection. Second, what Section 5.2 reports are patterns among Quina-bearing localities rather than a map of Quina technology across the two basins; since the visibility of surface localities depends on exposure, vegetation cover and survey intensity, these patterns are read here as trends and not as reality densities. The surface collections examined below have no independent age control, and the Longtan dates cannot be transferred to them: what those dates establish is when the Quina system was present in this landscape, not when any individual collection was formed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-localities
#| tbl-cap: "The Quina localities retained for analysis. Landform is the position within the terrace sequence, T2 the lowest terrace, with the three localities standing well above that sequence entered as hilltops. Coordinates are degrees, minutes and seconds, and elevation is metres above sea level. The last two columns give the assemblage on which the analyses below are based."

# rounds to 0.1 s before splitting, so no second can round up to 60
dms <- function(x, hemi) {
  tot <- round(x * 3600, 1)
  d   <- floor(tot / 3600)
  m   <- floor((tot - d * 3600) / 60)
  s   <- tot - d * 3600 - m * 60
  sprintf("%d°%02d′%04.1f″%s", d, m, s, hemi)
}

sites_tbl <- read_excel(here("data", "Site_information.xlsx"))
names(sites_tbl) <- trimws(names(sites_tbl))
sites_tbl <- sites_tbl |>
  transmute(name = gsub("_", " ", trimws(as.character(name))),
            # the data file names this basin after the county, the text after the basin
            basin = ifelse(grepl("^Heqing", trimws(basin)), "Huangping Basin", "Binchuan Basin"),
            valley = trimws(as.character(river_ID)),
            geomorph = trimws(as.character(geomorph)),
            lat = as.numeric(lat), lon = as.numeric(lon), elev = as.numeric(elev_m),
            n_sc = as.integer(n_Quina_scraper), n_rf = as.integer(n_Resharpening_flake))

loc_fmt <- bind_rows(lapply(c("Binchuan Basin", "Huangping Basin"), function(b) {
  s <- sites_tbl[sites_tbl$basin == b, ]
  bind_rows(
    data.frame(Locality = sprintf("**%s** (*n* = %d localities)", b, nrow(s)),
               valley = "", geomorph = "", lat = "", lon = "", elev = "",
               n_sc = as.character(sum(s$n_sc)), n_rf = as.character(sum(s$n_rf))),
    data.frame(Locality = paste0(IND, s$name), valley = s$valley, geomorph = s$geomorph,
               lat = dms(s$lat, "N"), lon = dms(s$lon, "E"), elev = as.character(s$elev),
               n_sc = as.character(s$n_sc), n_rf = as.character(s$n_rf)))
})) |>
  bind_rows(data.frame(Locality = "**Total**", valley = "", geomorph = "",
                       lat = "", lon = "", elev = "",
                       n_sc = as.character(sum(sites_tbl$n_sc)),
                       n_rf = as.character(sum(sites_tbl$n_rf))))

knitr::kable(loc_fmt, row.names = FALSE,
             align = c("l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Locality", "Valley", "Landform", "Latitude",
                           "Longitude", "Elevation (m)", "Quina scrapers",
                           "Resharpening flakes"))
```

## Techno-typological analysis of Quina retouch products

The techno-typological observations and measurements follow established practice in the study of Quina assemblages [@Bourguignon1997; @peresani2023; @ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a; @hiscock2008construction]. For each Quina scraper we recorded length, width, thickness and mass; cortex position; platform type and platform depth (PD); interior platform angle (IPA); the number of retouch generations; the numbers of convex scars and concave scars; the geometric index of unifacial reduction (GIUR) [@kuhnGeometricIndexReduction1990] and the proportion of the perimeter retouched; the edge angle; and its attribution within Bordes' type list [@bordes1961; @debenath1994]. For each resharpening flake we recorded dimensions, platform type, PD, IPA and exterior platform angle (EPA). Relationships between edge angle and GIUR, the proportion of retouched edge and the mean number of retouch generations were examined with Spearman rank correlation, with p-values adjusted by the Bonferroni procedure. The difference between the EPAs of the resharpening flakes and the edge angles of the scrapers was tested with Welch's t-test, so that unequal variances would not affect the inference [@welch1947generalization], and its magnitude summarised by Cohen's *d* with a bootstrap percentile confidence interval.

To test the technological consistency between the surface Quina scrapers and the excavated material, the Quina scrapers from Longtan were used as the reference, and non-Quina scrapers from the same site were included as a technological control group. To reduce dimensionality and minimise redundancy among correlated variables, six of the recorded variables were selected for multivariate analysis as the most representative: thickness, proportion of the perimeter retouched, GIUR, number of total scars, number of retouch generations and edge angle. All were standardised to z-scores and differences between specimens computed as Euclidean distances. Differences between groups were tested by permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) [@anderson2001new], with the proportion of variance explained (*R*²) reported for each pairwise comparison. The non-Quina scrapers serve to calibrate the scale on which those *R*² values are read: if the same set of variables separates Quina from ordinary scrapers with a high *R*² while the two Quina groups differ only at a low *R*², the latter is more likely to reflect a real technological similarity than a lack of statistical power. At the univariate level, mean GIUR, scar count and mean number of retouch generations were compared with Kruskal–Wallis rank sum tests followed by Dunn's post hoc comparisons, and thickness, proportion of the perimeter retouched and edge angle with Welch's ANOVA followed by Welch's t post hoc comparisons; all post hoc comparisons were corrected using the Bonferroni method. The distributions on which that choice of test rests are given in Fig. S3. Technological dispersion between groups was tested with PERMDISP [@andersonDistanceBasedTestsHomogeneity2006]. To compare the degree of variation within groups, the coefficients of variation (CV) of length, width, thickness, mass and edge angle were tested for equality across groups using the Krishnamoorthy–Lee modified signed likelihood ratio test (KL-MSLRT) [@krishnamoorthy2014], these being ratio-scale variables with a true zero. GIUR, the proportion of the perimeter retouched, number of total scars and the number of retouch generations were instead compared with Fligner–Killeen tests [@fligner1976]: the first two are bounded on \[0, 1\], which leaves the CV without a clear interpretation, and the last two are counts whose variance structure does not meet the assumptions required for comparing CVs. To assess how robust the results are, the analyses were repeated with the surface specimens collected from within the area of the Longtan site removed (Table S6, Fig. S4).

## Survey and analysis of raw materials

To establish what raw material was locally available, gravel bars were sampled at five points along three river channels (@fig-geology; Fig. S5). At each point an area of 1–2 m² was cleared and every cobble longer than 30 mm exposed at the surface was recorded. For each cobble we recorded length, width and thickness (mm), roundness on a four-point scale (angular, subangular, subrounded, well-rounded) and shape (sub-oval, tabular or irregular). Because the shape terms of the field record mix geometric form with regularity, form was not analysed from them but derived from the axes themselves: the three measurements of each cobble were sorted into *a* ≥ *b* ≥ *c* and treated as a composition, so that the comparison of form is invariant to size [@aitchison1986; @egozcue2003]. Form was compared between lithologies by PERMANOVA on Aitchison distances, with PERMDISP used to test the homogeneity of dispersions [@andersonDistanceBasedTestsHomogeneity2006]; because Aitchison distance does not depend on the choice of ilr basis, the result is unaffected by that choice. Cobbles were displayed on the ternary diagram of Sneed and Folk [-@sneed1958], with contours of maximum projection sphericity, (*c*²/*ab*)^1/3^. Size was represented by the geometric mean of the three axes and compared between lithologies with a Mann–Whitney U test [@erenRoleRawMaterial2014].

To characterise the internal properties of the dominant raw material, thin sections were prepared from five trachyte cobbles and examined petrographically, with mineral composition determined by energy-dispersive spectroscopy (@fig-thin-section). The raw material of each artefact was assigned macroscopically to the same lithological categories, using the surveyed cobbles as a reference collection.

Differences in raw material composition, both between the gravel bars and the artefacts and between spatial units, were tested by PERMANOVA, stratified at two scales, basin and valley.

Because the artefacts are made overwhelmingly on river cobbles, the straight-line distance from each locality to the nearest channel was used as a proxy for proximity to a source of raw material. These distances are strongly skewed, the groups differ considerably in size, and their variances are unequal, so differences between the two basins were tested with a Mann–Whitney U test and differences among the three valleys with a Kruskal–Wallis H test; medians are reported as the measure of central tendency and the rank tests taken as the primary criterion.

Raw material selection was quantified with Jacobs' electivity index *D* [@jacobs1974], a modification of Ivlev's index that corrects for the relative abundance of the available resources:

$$D = \frac{r - p}{\,r + p - 2\,r\,p\,}$$\$\$D = \\frac{r - p}{\\,r + p - 2\\,r\\,p\\,}\$\$

where *r* is the proportion of a given raw material among the artefacts and *p* is its proportion among the cobbles recorded in the gravel survey. *D* ranges from −1 (complete avoidance) through 0 (use in proportion to availability) to +1 (complete selection). It was computed for each raw material in the surface Quina scrapers against availability pooled across the gravel survey. Where either proportion is zero the index saturates: a material absent from the gravel survey returns *D* = +1, and one absent from the artefacts returns *D* = −1, whatever the value of the other proportion. In these cases *D* records the direction of the selection but not its strength, and a zero in the gravel survey is in any case a sampling zero rather than a demonstrated absence. Such values are therefore reported for completeness but are not read on the same scale as those computed from two non-zero proportions.

## Landscape structure

To test whether technological variation is systematically structured by the landscape, the analysis was repeated with the locality as the unit, each locality represented by the median value of its Quina scrapers on the same six variables. Four landscape variables were considered: basin (Huangping or Binchuan), the height of the locality above the present-day channel, distance from the locality to that channel, and assemblage size (number of specimens). Height above the channel was used in preference to a categorical terrace level, and in preference to absolute elevation: it is the continuous quantity of which terrace level is a discretisation, and because it is measured from the local channel rather than from sea level, the difference in base level between the two basins cancels out. Basin, the only categorical variable, was tested with PERMANOVA and PERMDISP; the three continuous variables with Spearman rank correlation, and with locality-level PERMANOVA on Euclidean distances.

All statistical analyses were carried out in R 4.5.2 [@rcoreteam2025]. Package versions, permutation, Monte Carlo and bootstrap settings, and the random seed are given in Supplementary Information.

## Reproducibility and open materials

Computational reproducibility remains a challenge in archaeological science, yet it underpins both the credibility of quantitative results and their re-use by others [@marwickComputationalReproducibilityArchaeological2017; @marwick2017openscience]. All materials needed to reproduce the analyses reported here are therefore available in a version-controlled online repository at \[\[OSF DOI\]\]. These comprise the raw data underlying every reported result together with the complete code used for the analyses and for the figures derived from them. The repository is organised with a logical folder structure and relative file paths, so that the code runs without manual modification.

The `r n_scraper` Quina scrapers from the surface collections are consistent with the Quina technological concept in each of its three dimensions: in the blanks selection, in the retouch strategy, in the ramification (Table S1).

(E) and (F) *limaces*. Note that the ventral face of the blank in (F) preserves previous centripetal removals, indicating that this specimen underwent different stages of functional transformation, that is “mixed-matrix”.](../figures/quina_scraper.png){#fig-quina-scrapers width="5.9in"}

[Blank selection.]{.underline} Quina flaking yields thick flakes with markedly asymmetric cross-sections (Section 2), and the blanks used here carry the attributes that this strategy produces (Fig. S2; further specimens are figured in Fig. S1). Most scrapers retain cortex to some degree (*n* = `r cortex_bearing_n`, `r f(cortex_bearing_pct, 1)`%), and where cortex survives it lies most often on a lateral margin (*n* = `r lateral_n` of `r cortex_bearing_n`, `r f(lateral_pct, 1)`%), opposite the retouched edge, forming a thick back. Some were made directly on cortical flakes, with cortex covering most of the dorsal face (*n* = `r primary_n`, `r f(primary_pct, 1)`%); among specimens without cortex, a lateral thick back usually formed by previous removals (*n* = `r nocortex_n`, `r f(nocortex_pct, 1)`%). The asymmetric distribution of volume is therefore present whether or not the original surface of the cobble survives. These are not ordinary flakes that happened to be retouched, but blanks carrying a reserve of volume that were selected by knappers.

Platform observations point the same way. In all, `r plat_n` Quina scrapers (`r f(plat_pct, 1)`%) retain the platform of the original blank, and these are characteristically wide and oblique, with a median platform depth of `r f(pd_median, 1)` mm (Q1–Q3 = `r f(pd_q1, 1)`–`r f(pd_q3, 1)` mm) and a mean IPA of `r f(ipa_mean, 0)`° (*SD* = `r f(ipa_sd, 1)`°); both follow from the invasive percussion by which thick blanks are removed by plan-secant flaking. Plain platforms predominate (*n* = `r plain_n`, `r f(plain_pct, 1)`%), with cortical (*n* = `r natural_n`, `r f(natural_pct, 1)`%) and dihedral platforms (*n* = `r dihedral_n`, `r f(dihedral_pct, 1)`%) less common (Fig. S2). Four of the dihedral specimens are *talons à pans*, on which the platform preserves parallel removal scars running approximately orthogonal to the axis of percussion. Few though they are, these carry the most direct information in the assemblage about the reduction strategy behind the blanks: a platform of this kind records a surface that had itself previously served as a flaking surface, which is what the alternating plan-secant exploitation.

<!-- TODO author: the sentence above is incomplete ("...which is what the alternating plan-secant exploitation [produces? entails?]"); the intended final word is ambiguous, so it is left unchanged. -->

[Edge maintenance.]{.underline} The convex-to-concave rhythm by which a Quina edge is sustained (Section 2) is clearly expressed in this assemblage. Quina scrapers carry a mean of `r f(rg_mean, 2)` retouch generations (*SD* = `r f(rg_sd, 2)`), with a mean of `r f(cxs_mean, 1)` convex scars (*SD* = `r f(cxs_sd, 1)`) and `r f(cvs_mean, 1)` concave scars (*SD* = `r f(cvs_sd, 1)`) per specimen. Convex scars are concentrated in the first generation, concave scars in the second and third. The imbalance between the two, better than four concave removals for every convex one, is the quantitative signature of an edge maintained far beyond its initial production.

Two measures quantify how far that process was carried. The GIUR has a median of `r f(giur_median, 2)` (Q1–Q3 = `r f(giur_q1, 2)`–`r f(giur_q3, 2)`), indicating that retouch commonly extended into the zone of maximum blank thickness; the proportion of the perimeter retouched has a median of `r f(rli_median, 2)` (Q1–Q3 = `r f(rli_q1, 2)`–`r f(rli_q3, 2)`), consistent with the thick back retained on most specimens. A minority were worked more extensively across the whole piece, among them the triple scrapers and *limaces*. Mean edge angle is `r f(ea_mean, 1)`° (*SD* = `r f(ea_sd, 1)`°). Because the angle produced by the final generation alone cannot be isolated, what we measured is the angle of the edge as a whole, and this is better read as an index of cumulative reduction than as a direct measure of function [@linQuinaRetouchDoes2021]; edge angle shows significant positive correlation with GIUR (ρ = `r f(ea_giur["rho"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(ea_giur["p"])`), with the proportion of the perimeter retouched (ρ = `r f(ea_rli["rho"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(ea_rli["p"])`) and with the number of retouch generations (ρ = `r f(ea_rg["rho"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(ea_rg["p"])`) (@fig-edge-angle-reduction), which supports that reading.

```{r}
#| label: fig-edge-angle-reduction
#| fig-cap: "Relationship between Quina scraper edge angle and three measures (proportion of perimeter retouched, GIUR, and number of retouch generations). Each panel reports Spearman’s ρ and p-value. The dashed line represents an ordinary least-squares linear fit, shown only as a visual guide to the direction of the relationship."
#| fig-width: 5.9
#| fig-height: 2.44

set.seed(2226)
focal_ea    <- "Edge_Angle"
corr_vars   <- c("Retouch_length_index", "Ave_GIUR", "Ave_RG")
corr_labels <- c(Retouch_length_index = "Retouched perimeter",
                 Ave_GIUR = "GIUR", Ave_RG = "Retouch generations")
fmt_p_math  <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "italic(p) < 0.001",
                                  sprintf("italic(p) == %.3f", p))

quina_ea <- read_excel(sc_path, sheet = "Quina scraper") |>
  mutate(across(all_of(c(focal_ea, corr_vars)), as.numeric))
spearman_one <- function(v) {
  pair <- quina_ea |> select(all_of(c(focal_ea, v))) |> drop_na()
  ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(pair[[focal_ea]], pair[[v]], method = "spearman", exact = FALSE))
  data.frame(Variable = v, rho = unname(ct$estimate), p_value = ct$p.value)
}
results_ea <- do.call(rbind, lapply(corr_vars, spearman_one))
results_ea$p_value <- p.adjust(results_ea$p_value, "bonferroni")   # one family of three

long_ea <- quina_ea |> select(all_of(c(focal_ea, corr_vars))) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(corr_vars), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") |>
  filter(!is.na(.data[[focal_ea]]), !is.na(Value)) |>
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = corr_vars),
         x_plot = if_else(Variable == "Ave_RG", Value + runif(n(), -0.11, 0.11), Value))
labels_ea <- results_ea |>
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = corr_vars),
         label = sprintf("rho == %.2f * ',' ~ %s", rho, fmt_p_math(p_value)))

fig_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E6E8EB", linewidth = 0.3),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#202124", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
        axis.ticks = element_line(color = "#202124", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(2, "pt"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 9), axis.text = element_text(color = "#303238", size = 8),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#202124", size = 8.5),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#E8E8E8", color = NA),
        plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"),
        panel.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"))

ggplot(long_ea, aes(y = .data[[focal_ea]])) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = Value), method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
              color = "#6BA8CE", fill = "#CBDCEA", linewidth = 0.6, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(x = x_plot), color = "#565693", alpha = 0.5, size = 1.4, shape = 16) +
  geom_text(data = labels_ea, aes(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = label), parse = TRUE,
            hjust = -0.08, vjust = 1.35, size = 2.5, color = "#202124", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3, labeller = as_labeller(corr_labels)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.14))) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.06)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Edge angle (°)") +
  fig_theme + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank())
```

Within this common scheme the Quina scrapers vary typologically: `r styp_n["Single"]` of them (`r f(styp_p["Single"], 1)`%) carry retouch on a single edge, `r styp_n["Double"]` (`r f(styp_p["Double"], 1)`%) on two, and `r styp_n["Multi"]` (`r f(styp_p["Multi"], 1)`%) on three or more, and their attributions across Bordes' type list are given in @tbl-bordes-typology. Since every specimen conforms to the Quina retouch, this variation is more plausibly a matter of knappers adjusting to the blanks in front of them than evidence of distinct technological concept [@hiscock2008construction].

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bordes-typology
#| tbl-cap: "Attribution of the surface Quina scrapers within Bordes' type list, grouped by type family. The triple scraper is not a type of Bordes' list and is entered without a number."

# the two orderings of the straight/convex double scraper are one Bordes type
bordes <- gsub("\\s+", " ", trimws(as.character(q$Bordes_typology)))
bordes[bordes == "Double convex-straight scraper"] <- "Double straight-convex scraper"

bordes_key <- tribble(
  ~family,                          ~no,  ~short,            ~recorded,
  "Simple scrapers",                "9",  "straight",        "Single straight scraper",
  "Simple scrapers",                "10", "convex",          "Single convex scraper",
  "Simple scrapers",                "11", "concave",         "Single concave scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "12", "straight",        "Double straight scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "13", "straight–convex", "Double straight-convex scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "15", "biconvex",        "Double convex scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "16", "biconcave",       "Double concave scraper",
  "Double scrapers",                "17", "convex–concave",  "Double convex-concave scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "18", "straight",        "Straight convergent scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "19", "convex",          "Convex convergent scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "20", "concave",         "Concave convergent scraper",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "21", "déjeté",          "Déjeté scraper",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "22", "straight",        "Straight transverse scraper",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "23", "convex",          "Convex transverse scraper",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "24", "concave",         "Concave transverse scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "25", "inverse",         "Inverse scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "29", "alternate",       "Alternate scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "28", "bifacial",        "Bifacial scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "—",  "triple",          "Triple scraper",
  "Other forms",                    "8",  "limace",          "Limace")
bordes_fam <- tribble(
  ~family,                          ~no_range,
  "Simple scrapers",                "9–11",
  "Double scrapers",                "12–17",
  "Convergent and déjeté scrapers", "18–21",
  "Transverse scrapers",            "22–24",
  "Other forms",                    "")
# a label recorded outside the key would drop specimens from the table
stopifnot(setequal(unique(bordes), bordes_key$recorded))

bordes_key$n <- vapply(bordes_key$recorded, function(l) sum(bordes == l), integer(1))
pc <- function(x) f(100 * x / length(bordes), 1)

bordes_tbl <- bind_rows(lapply(bordes_fam$family, function(fm) {
  k <- bordes_key[bordes_key$family == fm, ]
  bind_rows(
    data.frame(Type = sprintf("**%s**", fm),
               no = bordes_fam$no_range[bordes_fam$family == fm],
               n = sum(k$n), pct = pc(sum(k$n))),
    data.frame(Type = paste0(IND, k$short), no = k$no, n = k$n, pct = pc(k$n)))
})) |>
  bind_rows(data.frame(Type = "**Total**", no = "", n = length(bordes), pct = f(100, 1)))

knitr::kable(bordes_tbl, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Bordes type", "No.", "*n*", "%"))
```

[Ramification sequence.]{.underline} The resharpening flakes (*n* = `r rf_n`) support the reading of the retouch just described and, at the same time, document the third dimension of the Quina system. They are characteristically flat and oval in plan with an arched profile, and the proximal part of their dorsal face preserves scars of previous Quina retouch (@fig-resharpening-flakes); their platforms are shallow (mean PD = `r f(rf_pd_mean, 1)` mm, *SD* = `r f(rf_pd_sd, 1)` mm), as marginal percussion produces. Their EPAs average `r f(epa_mean, 1)`° (*SD* = `r f(epa_sd, 1)`°), compared with a mean edge angle of `r f(ea_mean, 1)`° on the Quina scrapers. Although this difference approached significance (Welch's *t* = `r f(welch_t, 2)`, *df* = `r f(welch_df, 1)`, *p* `r fp(welch_p)`), its magnitude was small, with a Cohen's *d* of `r f(cohd, 2)` (95% CI: `r f(cohd_lo, 2)` to `r f(cohd_hi, 2)`), indicating only a limited separation between Quina scrapers' edge angle and resharpening flakes' EPAs. Since the EPA of a resharpening flake records the angle of the edge from which it was struck, the near identity of the two distributions is what would be expected if these flakes had been detached from Quina scrapers of the kind recovered alongside them; the small residual offset falls within the range that uneven sampling across surface localities would produce, and need not indicate a systematic difference in the angle at which edges were reworked.

![Quina resharpening flakes from the surface collections. Note that in (E) and (F), the flake technological axes are nearly orthogonal to the dorsal retouch directions of the associated Quina scraper edges, indicating variability in edge maintenance strategies.](../figures/resharpening_flake.png){#fig-resharpening-flakes width="5.9in"}

Ramification extends beyond the maintenance of edges. Resharpening flakes carry cutting edges of their own and were therefore usable as struck (Section 2); some Quina scrapers additionally bear "Clactonian notch" removals struck from the edge: broad, invasive scars whose corresponding resharpening flakes are larger, and which are therefore themselves candidates for further modification [@peresani2023]. Material already in hand was thus drawn on repeatedly, first to restore a working edge and then to yield fresh blanks from the tool itself.

### Technological consistency

[Consistency with Longtan.]{.underline} The surface Quina scrapers cannot be distinguished from the excavated Quina scrapers at Longtan (*n* = `r ltq_n`), while both are clearly separated from the non-Quina scrapers (*n* = `r lto_n`) that serve as a control. In the technological space, PERMANOVA finds no difference between the two Quina groups (*R*² = `r f(tc_scltq_R2, 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(tc_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(tc_scltq_p)`), whereas each differs from the non-Quina scrapers with an order of magnitude more explained variance (*R*² = `r f(min(tc_nonq_R2), 2)`–`r f(max(tc_nonq_R2), 2)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(min(tc_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(tc_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(tc_nonq_p)` in both cases) (@fig-technological-consistency; Table S2). The loadings of the ordination in @fig-technological-consistency are given in full in Table S5.

```{r}
#| label: fig-technological-consistency
#| fig-cap: "Technological consistency of surface Quina scrapers with the excavated Longtan Quina scrapers, against Longtan non-Quina scrapers as a control, on six technological variables. (A) PCA of the z-scored technological space, with convex hulls, group centroids, variable loadings, and marginal histograms of the PC1 and PC2 scores by group. (B) Per-variable distributions with pairwise post-hoc brackets."
#| fig-width: 5.9
#| fig-height: 8.07

group_colors <- c(SC_Quina = "#E07C90", LT_Quina = "#E6C25C", LT_Ordinary = "#6BA8CE")
group_labels <- c(SC_Quina = "Surface Quina", LT_Quina = "Longtan Quina",
                  LT_Ordinary = "Longtan non-Quina")

fig_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E6E8EB", linewidth = 0.3),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#202124", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
        axis.ticks = element_line(color = "#202124", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(2, "pt"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 9), axis.text = element_text(color = "#303238", size = 8),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#202124", size = 8.5),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#E8E8E8", color = NA),
        legend.title = element_blank(), legend.text = element_text(size = 8.5),
        legend.key = element_blank(), plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"),
        panel.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"))

scores   <- tc$pca_scores
loadings <- tc$pca_loadings
vexp     <- tc$var_explained
centroids <- scores |> group_by(Group) |> summarise(cx = mean(PC1), cy = mean(PC2), .groups = "drop")
hulls <- scores |> group_by(Group) |> filter(n() >= 3) |>
  group_modify(function(g, k) { h <- chull(g$PC1, g$PC2); bind_rows(g[h, ], g[h[1], ]) }) |> ungroup()
arrow_mult <- 0.85 * min(max(abs(scores$PC1)) / max(abs(loadings$PC1)),
                         max(abs(scores$PC2)) / max(abs(loadings$PC2)))
arrows_df <- loadings |> mutate(x = PC1 * arrow_mult, y = PC2 * arrow_mult,
                                Label = variable_labels_bare[Variable])
EXP_X <- expansion(mult = 0.20); EXP_Y <- expansion(mult = 0.10)

p_a <- ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, PC2, color = Group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey55") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3, color = "grey55") +
  geom_polygon(data = hulls, aes(fill = Group, group = Group), alpha = 0.12, color = NA) +
  geom_path(data = hulls, aes(group = Group), linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_point(size = 1.1, alpha = 0.7, shape = 16) +
  geom_point(data = centroids, aes(cx, cy, fill = Group), shape = 21, color = "#5A5F66",
             size = 2.4, stroke = 0.6, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_segment(data = arrows_df, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.075, "cm"), type = "open", angle = 22),
               linewidth = 0.22, color = "#5A5F66", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_text_repel(data = arrows_df, aes(x = x, y = y, label = Label),
               size = 2.2, color = "#3A3D42", bg.color = "white", bg.r = 0.12,
               segment.color = "grey55", segment.size = 0.2, min.segment.length = 0.2,
               box.padding = 0.35, point.padding = 0.1, max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 2226,
               inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_colors, labels = group_labels) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors, labels = group_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = EXP_X) + scale_y_continuous(expand = EXP_Y) +
  labs(x = sprintf("PC1 (%.1f%%)", vexp[1]), y = sprintf("PC2 (%.1f%%)", vexp[2])) +
  fig_theme +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), legend.position = "inside",
        legend.position.inside = c(0.995, 0.995), legend.justification = c(1, 1),
        legend.background = element_rect(fill = alpha("white", 0.85), color = NA),
        legend.margin = margin(2, 4, 2, 2), legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
        legend.key.height = unit(8, "pt")) +
  guides(fill = "none", color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 1.6, alpha = 1), ncol = 1))

marg_theme <- theme_void() +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA), plot.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0))
p_mx <- ggplot(scores, aes(PC1, after_stat(density), fill = Group, color = Group)) +
  geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.25, bins = 26) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors) + scale_color_manual(values = group_colors) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = EXP_X) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  marg_theme + guides(fill = "none", color = "none")
p_my <- ggplot(scores, aes(y = PC2, after_stat(density), fill = Group, color = Group)) +
  geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 0.25, bins = 22) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = group_colors) + scale_color_manual(values = group_colors) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = EXP_Y) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  marg_theme + guides(fill = "none", color = "none")

p_b <- ggplot(tc$variable_long, aes(Group, Value)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = Group), width = 0.3, height = 0, size = 0.8, alpha = 0.5, shape = 16) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "black", fill = NA, width = 0.6, linewidth = 0.45, outlier.shape = NA) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = 16, size = 1.4, color = "black") +
  stat_pvalue_manual(tc$posthoc_brackets, label = "p.adj.signif", y.position = "y.position",
     tip.length = 0.012, bracket.size = 0.3, label.size = 2.5, color = "#202124") +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3, labeller = as_labeller(variable_labels)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = group_colors, labels = group_labels) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = group_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.12))) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  fig_theme + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1, size = 7.5)) +
  guides(color = "none")

top_row <- (p_mx + labs(tag = "A") + theme(plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))) +
  plot_spacer() + p_a + p_my +
  plot_layout(design = "AB\nCD", widths = c(5, 1), heights = c(1, 5.5))
top_row / (p_b + labs(tag = "B")) + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.5))
```

The control group is what makes this result interpretable. A non-significant difference is not enough by itself evidence of similarity: it may equally reflect variables too blunt to separate anything, or a sample too small to detect what is there. Because the same six variables separate Quina from non-Quina scrapers with relative higher *R*², they are demonstrably capable of resolving technological differences of the kind at issue here. What this establishes is not that the two groups are identical, which no test can show, but that any difference between them is far smaller than the difference that distinguishes Quina from non-Quina scrapers work.

The univariate results follow the same pattern. None of the six variables differs between the two Quina groups, while every one of them differs between each Quina group and the non-Quina scrapers (@fig-technological-consistency; Table S4). Agreement therefore holds not only in the multi-dimension technological space but in each of its component measures.

Consistency of this kind concerns the position of group centroids, and two assemblages could share a centroid while differing in how widely they vary around it. PERMDISP shows that they do not. The mean distance to centroid is almost the same in the two Quina groups (`r f(pd_scq, 2)` and `r f(pd_ltq, 2)`; *F* = `r f(permdisp_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(permdisp_scltq_p)`), whereas the non-Quina scrapers are less dispersed (`r f(pd_lto, 2)`) and differ significantly from both (*F* = `r f(min(permdisp_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(permdisp_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(permdisp_nonq_p)` in each case; Table S3). Here again the control group establishes that the analysis can detect a real difference in dispersion where one exists, so that the absence of such a difference between the Quina groups is not a matter of sensitivity. The univariate dispersion tests agree: neither the KL-MSLRT nor the Fligner–Killeen tests detect any difference in variability between the two Quina groups (@tbl-dispersion-tests), and every dispersion ratio has a confidence interval containing one.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dispersion-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Univariate dispersion of the surface Quina scrapers against the Longtan Quina scrapers. Each family is summarised by the dispersion measure appropriate to its scale of measurement and tested by the corresponding procedure; the ratio is surface over Longtan, so that one denotes equal dispersion, and its interval is a bootstrap percentile interval. The statistic is the MSLRT for the coefficient of variation and the Fligner–Killeen chi-squared elsewhere."

disp_heads <- c(CV      = "Coefficient of variation (CV\\*), KL-MSLRT",
                bounded = "Median absolute deviation, Fligner–Killeen",
                count   = "Fano factor, Fligner–Killeen")
fd <- function(x) ifelse(abs(x) < 1, f(x, 3), f(x, 2))

disp_fmt <- bind_rows(lapply(names(disp_heads), function(fam) {
  d <- disp_tests[disp_tests$family == fam, ]
  bind_rows(
    data.frame(Variable = sprintf("**%s**", disp_heads[[fam]]),
               sc = "", lt = "", ratio = "", stat = "", p = ""),
    data.frame(Variable = paste0(IND, disp_labels[d$variable]),
               sc = fd(d$sc), lt = fd(d$lt),
               ratio = sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", f(d$ratio, 2), f(d$lo, 2), f(d$hi, 2)),
               stat = fd(d$stat), p = sub("^= ", "", vapply(d$p, fp, character(1)))))
}))

knitr::kable(disp_fmt, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Variable", "Surface", "Longtan", "Ratio (95% CI)",
                           "Statistic", "*p*"))
```

These results are not driven by the material belongs to Longtan surface collections. Repeating the analyses with the surface specimens collected from within the area of the site removed leaves them unchanged (Table S6; Fig. S4). The two Quina groups remain indistinguishable both in centroid position (*R*² = `r f(sens_perm_scltq_R2, 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(sens_perm_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(sens_perm_scltq_p)`) and in dispersion (*F* = `r f(sens_scltq_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(sens_scltq_p)`), while both remain separated from the non-Quina scrapers in centroid position (*R*² = `r f(min(sens_perm_nonq_R2), 3)`–`r f(max(sens_perm_nonq_R2), 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(min(sens_perm_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(sens_perm_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(sens_perm_nonq_p)`) and significantly more dispersed than them (*F* = `r f(min(sens_nonq_F), 1)`–`r f(max(sens_nonq_F), 1)`, *p* `r fp(sens_nonq_p)`). The agreement documented here therefore reflects the surface collections as a whole rather than a single locality or a local peculiarity of sampling.

Taken together, in centroid position and in dispersion alike, the surface Quina scrapers and the excavated Quina scrapers from Longtan cannot be told apart on measurements that readily separate both from other retouched scrapers at the same site. They are most economically understood as the products of a single technological concept.

## Raw material economy and landscape organisation

The preceding section established the technological identity of the entity; this one asks how it was organised across the landscape. Quina localities in both basins lie along the valley systems, on river terraces, and at consistently short distances from the channels. In the Huangping Basin they are concentrated on the second and third terraces; in the Binchuan Basin they extend across the second to fourth terraces (T2–T4), with a small number (*n* = 3) occurring higher, on hilltops. Because the artefacts are made overwhelmingly on river cobbles, the straight-line distance from a locality to the nearest channel serves as a proxy for ease of access to lithic raw material. Across the three valleys, the Sangyuan, Liandong and Caifeng, these distances are short and similarly distributed, with a median of `r f(dist_median, 0)` m. Neither comparison detected a difference between spatial units, whether at the scale of the basin (*U* = `r f(dist_basin_U, 0)`, *p* `r fp(dist_basin_p)`) or of the valley (*H* = `r f(dist_river_H, 2)`, *df* = `r dist_river_df`, *p* `r fp(dist_river_p)`). Access to river gravels therefore appears to have been broadly comparable across the study area, so that differences in the raw materials actually used at these localities are unlikely to be explained by differential proximity to a source.

Raw material use does not follow raw material abundance. On the gravel bars, sandstone is the most abundant lithology (`r f(sand_avail_pct, 1)`% of `r n_cobble` cobbles), with trachyte second (`r f(trach_avail_pct, 1)`%); among the artefacts, trachyte accounts for `r f(trach_used_pct, 1)`% (Table S7). The bars are not uniform in composition, however: raw material composition differs significantly between sampling points (*R*² = `r f(cobbleLoc_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(cobbleLoc_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(cobbleLoc_v["p"])`), and stratified analysis attributes this variation to differences between valleys (*R*² = `r f(cobbleRiver_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(cobbleRiver_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(cobbleRiver_v["p"])`) rather than within them (Table S9). Sandstone-dominated and trachyte-richer bars are therefore distributed unevenly across the study area, in a pattern that follows the contrast in bedrock described in Section 3 (@fig-geology). If knappers had simply worked whatever lay most abundantly at hand, the raw material composition of the artefacts should vary from valley to valley in the same way.

That expectation is not met. The raw material composition of the Quina scrapers is uniform across the study area, differing neither between basins (*R*² = `r f(usedA_basin_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(usedA_basin_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(usedA_basin_v["p"])`) nor between valleys (*R*² = `r f(usedA_river_v["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(usedA_river_v["F"], 2)`, *p* `r fp(usedA_river_v["p"])`) (@fig-raw-material-composition; Table S9). The same material was selected wherever knappers used, although sandstone is more abundant on the bars and although the composition of those bars varies from valley to valley. Jacobs' electivity index puts the strength of that preference on a common scale (Table S8): trachyte is strongly selected (*D* = `r f(D_trach, 2)`) and sandstone strongly avoided (*D* = `r f(D_sand, 2)`), with quartz and mudstone likewise avoided (*D* = `r f(D_quartz, 2)` in each case, neither being used at all); andesite returns *D* = `r f(D_and, 2)`, but only because the `r andesite_n` andesite artefacts have no counterpart among the recorded cobbles, so that its index is undefined in practice rather than informative. Because D returns to zero only when a raw material is used in proportion to its availability, trachyte would have to make up some `r f(trach_used_pct, 0)`% of the gravel before its use could be read as neutral; no redistribution of availability among the valleys approaches that figure, so neither the direction nor the magnitude of the selection depends on how availability is pooled. The selection of trachyte, in other words, was made against local abundance rather than in step with it.

```{r}

The sample size of each cell is given at the end of its bar."

valley_order <- rev(river_levels)
counts_lab <- transform(counts_fig, label = paste0("n = ", N))

ggplot(comp_fig, aes(percent, river_ID, fill = Material)) +
```
