
Two properties of the trachyte account for this preference, and a third can be excluded. Trachyte cobbles are significantly larger than sandstone cobbles (GM = `r f(gmT, 1)` mm against `r f(gmS, 1)` mm; *U* = `r f(size_U, 0)`, *p* `r fp(size_p)`; Table S10), giving a greater initial volume from which to sustain prolonged reduction. Their form does not distinguish them: treating the three axes as a composition, so that the comparison is invariant to size, the two lithologies are indistinguishable on Aitchison distances (*R*² = `r f(form_R2, 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(form_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(form_p)`), with no difference in dispersion (PERMDISP *F* = `r f(form_disp_F, 2)`, *p* `r fp(form_disp_p)`), and they occupy the same region of the Sneed and Folk form triangle (@fig-cobble-size-form). The preference cannot therefore have turned on the shapes in which the two raw materials occur on the bars. What remains is fracture predictability. In thin section the trachyte is porphyritic, with euhedral tabular to prismatic K-feldspar phenocrysts (\~0.3–5.0 mm, \~1–10% of the rock) set in a hyalopilitic groundmass of K-feldspar microlites, chlorite or altered mafic minerals, magnetite and about 50% devitrified glass (@fig-thin-section). Assessed on the criteria conventionally applied to volcanic rock, groundmass texture together with the size and abundance of phenocrysts [@stoutRawMaterialSelectivity2005], it is a fine-grained rock with a low phenocryst content, properties associated elsewhere with predictable conchoidal fracture and hence with long, continuous and acute edges. Size and fracture quality are the two properties on which prolonged resharpening most directly depends.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cobble-size-form
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of size and form between trachyte and sandstone cobbles from river gravels. (A) Comparison of cobble size between trachyte and sandstone, expressed as the geometric mean of length, width, and thickness on a logarithmic scale. Boxes indicate the median and interquartile range, whiskers extend to 1.5 times the interquartile range, and filled circles represent mean values. (B) Sneed–Folk ternary diagram showing the form distribution of the same cobbles. Trachyte and sandstone are plotted separately on two identical triangles. The three vertices represent the three end-member forms: compact, platy, and elongate. Statistical significance in (A) is indicated as follows: ns, not significant; * p < 0.05; ** p < 0.01; *** p < 0.001; **** p < 0.0001."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 2.63

# fig-height is set so the fixed-aspect ternary panel exactly fills its cell,
# which stops it being centred; reset it if the width or the layout changes.
#
material_colors_fig <- c(Trachyte = "#E07C90", Sandstone = "#6BA8CE",
                         Quartz = "#E6C25C", Mudstone = "#9B87C4", Andesite = "#6FB98E")

fig_theme <- theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#E6E8EB", linewidth = 0.3),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "#202124", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
        axis.ticks = element_line(color = "#202124", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.ticks.length = unit(2, "pt"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 9), axis.text = element_text(color = "#303238", size = 8),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#202124", size = 8.5),
        strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#E8E8E8", color = NA),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 8.5), legend.text = element_text(size = 8.5),
        legend.key = element_blank(), legend.key.size = unit(10, "pt"),
        plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
        plot.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"),
        panel.background = element_rect(color = NA, fill = "white"))

# the frame is one rectangle drawn inside the panel, so that its foot lands on
# the base of the triangles rather than on the foot of the panel: f_base is
# where that base sits, as a fraction of the ternary panel's height
tri_h     <- sqrt(3) / 2               # height of the unit equilateral triangle
tern_ylim <- c(-0.235, tri_h + 0.34)   # the ternary panels use these limits
f_base    <- -tern_ylim[1] / diff(tern_ylim)
frame_lwd  <- 0.4
# the height of a real strip, measured rather than guessed, so the two headings
# of (B) match those of the composition figure whatever the figure is scaled to
strip_pt  <- local({
  g <- ggplotGrob(ggplot(data.frame(x = 1, f = levels(sz$G)[1]), aes(x, x)) +
                    facet_wrap(~ f) + fig_theme)
  convertHeight(g$heights[g$layout$t[grepl("^strip-t", g$layout$name)][1]],
                "pt", valueOnly = TRUE)
})
frame_grob <- rectGrob(x = unit(0.5, "npc"), y = unit(f_base, "npc"),
                       width = unit(1, "npc"), height = unit(1 - f_base, "npc"),
                       just = c("centre", "bottom"),
                       gp = gpar(col = "#202124", fill = NA,
                                 lwd = frame_lwd * .pt, lineend = "square"))

size_gm  <- sz |> group_by(G) |> summarise(size = gm(size), .groups = "drop")
size_br  <- max(sz$size) * 1.06        # bracket height, clear of the largest clast
sz_span  <- log10(size_br) - log10(min(sz$size))
base_y   <- log10(min(sz$size)) - 0.05 * sz_span   # the baseline, in log10 mm
top_y    <- log10(size_br)        + 0.10 * sz_span
low_y    <- base_y - f_base / (1 - f_base) * (top_y - base_y)

p_size <- ggplot(sz, aes(G, size)) +
  geom_jitter(aes(color = G), size = 0.9, alpha = 0.35, shape = 16,
              position = position_jitter(width = 0.24, height = 0, seed = 2226)) +
  geom_boxplot(color = "#202124", fill = NA, width = 0.55, linewidth = 0.4,
               outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point(data = size_gm, shape = 16, size = 1.8, color = "#202124") +
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 2, y = size_br, yend = size_br,
           linewidth = 0.3, color = "#202124") +
  annotate("segment", x = c(1, 2), xend = c(1, 2), y = size_br, yend = size_br * 0.94,
           linewidth = 0.3, color = "#202124") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = size_br, label = psig(size_p),
           vjust = 0.1, size = 2.8, color = "#202124") +
  annotate("segment", x = c(1, 2), xend = c(1, 2), y = 10^base_y,
           yend = 10^(base_y - 0.017 * (top_y - low_y)),
           linewidth = frame_lwd, color = "#202124") +
  annotate("text", x = c(1, 2), y = 10^(base_y - 0.054 * (top_y - low_y)),
           label = c("Trachyte", "Sandstone"), vjust = 1,
           size = 2.4, color = "#303238") +
  # given in full: the infinite default is NaN through a log scale
  annotation_custom(frame_grob, xmin = 0.4, xmax = 2.6,
                    ymin = 10^low_y, ymax = 10^top_y) +
  scale_color_manual(values = material_colors_fig, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Trachyte", "Sandstone")) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(25, 50, 100, 200, 400),
                limits = 10^c(low_y, top_y), expand = expansion(0)) +
  coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Geometric mean size (mm)") +
  fig_theme + theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
                    panel.border = element_blank(),
                    axis.line = element_blank(),
                    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
                    axis.ticks.y = element_line(color = "#202124",
                                                linewidth = frame_lwd),
                    axis.text.x = element_blank())

to_xy  <- function(compact, elongate) {  # barycentric -> plane
  data.frame(x = elongate + compact / 2, y = tri_h * compact)
}
tri_out <- rbind(to_xy(0, 0), to_xy(0, 1), to_xy(1, 0), to_xy(0, 0))
sf_pts  <- cbind(to_xy(sz$sf_compact, sz$sf_elongate), G = sz$G)

ca_cuts <- c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7)                 # c/a
ab_cuts <- c(1 / 3, 2 / 3)                  # (a - b)/(a - c)
ca_top  <- max(ca_cuts)                     # the apex field is not subdivided
grid_ca <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ca_cuts, function(k)
  data.frame(g = paste0("ca", k), x = c(k / 2, 1 - k / 2), y = tri_h * k)))
grid_ab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(ab_cuts, function(t)
  data.frame(g = paste0("ab", round(t, 2)),
             x = c(t, (1 - ca_top) * t + ca_top / 2),
             y = c(0, tri_h * ca_top))))

gx  <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 300)
gy  <- seq(0, tri_h, length.out = 260)
grd <- expand.grid(x = gx, y = gy)
grd <- transform(grd, compact = y / tri_h)
grd <- transform(grd, elongate = x - compact / 2)
grd <- transform(grd, platy = 1 - compact - elongate,
                 ba_ratio = 1 - (x - compact / 2))          # b/a
grd$psi <- with(grd, ifelse(compact >= 0 & elongate >= 0 & platy >= 0 &
                              ba_ratio > 0,
                            (compact^2 / ba_ratio)^(1 / 3), NA_real_))
psi_lines <- contourLines(gx, gy, matrix(grd$psi, length(gx), length(gy)),
                          levels = seq(0.3, 0.9, by = 0.2))
psi_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(psi_lines), function(i)
  data.frame(g = i, level = psi_lines[[i]]$level,
             x = psi_lines[[i]]$x, y = psi_lines[[i]]$y)))

n_out    <- c(-tri_h, 0.5)                  # outward normal of the left edge
ca_ticks <- c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1)          # 0 is carried by the base scale
tick_ca  <- data.frame(x0 = ca_ticks / 2, y0 = tri_h * ca_ticks,
                       label = formatC(ca_ticks, format = "f", digits = 1))
tick_ca  <- transform(tick_ca,
                      x1 = x0 + 0.030 * n_out[1], y1 = y0 + 0.030 * n_out[2],
                      xl = x0 + 0.070 * n_out[1], yl = y0 + 0.070 * n_out[2])
ab_ticks <- c(0, 1 / 3, 2 / 3, 1)
tick_ab  <- data.frame(x0 = ab_ticks, y0 = 0, x1 = ab_ticks, y1 = -0.030,
                       xl = ab_ticks, yl = -0.072,
                       label = c("0", "0.33", "0.67", "1.0"))
vert_lab <- data.frame(
  x = c(0, 1, 0.5), y = c(-0.175, -0.175, tri_h + 0.105),
  label = c("Platy", "Elongate", "Compact"), vj = c(1, 1, 0))

# one panel, not two facets: facets nest inside the panel row and no longer
# align with (A). Everything is therefore drawn twice, shifted by tri_dx.
tri_dx <- 1.30
two <- function(d, xcols, gcol = NULL) {
  right <- d
  for (nm in xcols) right[[nm]] <- right[[nm]] + tri_dx
  if (!is.null(gcol)) {
    d[[gcol]] <- paste0(d[[gcol]], "_l"); right[[gcol]] <- paste0(right[[gcol]], "_r")
  }
  rbind(d, right)
}
tri_out$g  <- "o"
psi_df$g   <- as.character(psi_df$g)
sf_pts$x   <- sf_pts$x + ifelse(sf_pts$G == levels(sz$G)[2], tri_dx, 0)
# each heading is a bar of strip height hung from the top of the panel, with its
# label centred in it; both are absolute, so neither moves when the figure does
head_grob <- function(label) {
  grobTree(rectGrob(y = unit(1, "npc"), height = unit(strip_pt, "pt"),
                    just = c("centre", "top"),
                    gp = gpar(fill = "#E8E8E8", col = NA)),
           textGrob(label, y = unit(1, "npc") - unit(strip_pt / 2, "pt"),
                    gp = gpar(fontface = "bold", fontsize = 8.5, col = "#202124")))
}

p_form <- ggplot(sf_pts, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(data = two(psi_df, "x", "g"), aes(x, y, group = g),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.22, linetype = "22",
            colour = "#C3C8CE") +
  geom_line(data = two(grid_ca, "x", "g"), aes(x, y, group = g),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.22, linetype = "22",
            colour = "#9AA0A6") +
  geom_line(data = two(grid_ab, "x", "g"), aes(x, y, group = g),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = 0.22, linetype = "22",
            colour = "#9AA0A6") +
  geom_path(data = two(tri_out, "x", "g"), aes(x, y, group = g),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, linewidth = frame_lwd, colour = "#202124") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = G), size = 1.0, alpha = 0.55, shape = 16) +
  geom_segment(data = two(rbind(tick_ca[, c("x0", "y0", "x1", "y1")],
                                tick_ab[, c("x0", "y0", "x1", "y1")]),
                          c("x0", "x1")),
               aes(x = x0, y = y0, xend = x1, yend = y1), inherit.aes = FALSE,
               linewidth = frame_lwd, colour = "#202124") +
  geom_text(data = two(tick_ca, "xl"), aes(xl, yl, label = label),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.4, colour = "#303238",
            hjust = 1, vjust = 0.4) +
  geom_text(data = two(tick_ab, "xl"), aes(xl, yl, label = label),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.4, colour = "#303238", vjust = 1) +
  geom_text(data = two(vert_lab, "x"), aes(x, y, label = label, vjust = vj),
            inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 2.5, colour = "#5A5F66") +
  annotation_custom(head_grob(levels(sz$G)[1]), xmin = 0, xmax = 1,
                    ymin = tern_ylim[1], ymax = tern_ylim[2]) +
  annotation_custom(head_grob(levels(sz$G)[2]), xmin = tri_dx, xmax = 1 + tri_dx,
                    ymin = tern_ylim[1], ymax = tern_ylim[2]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = material_colors_fig, guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-0.17, 1.13 + tri_dx), ylim = tern_ylim,
              expand = FALSE, clip = "off") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  fig_theme +
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), panel.border = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())

(p_size + labs(tag = "A")) + (p_form + labs(tag = "B")) +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1.1, 3))
```

![Petrography of the trachyte. (A) Hand specimens of five of the sampled trachyte cobbles. (B) Photomicrographs of thin sections cut from them, with the magnification and the scale given in each frame. The rock is porphyritic: euhedral tabular to prismatic K-feldspar phenocrysts, with subordinate quartz, augite and clay minerals, are set in a fine-grained groundmass of K-feldspar microlites and devitrified glass.](../figures/thin_section.png){#fig-thin-section width="5.9in"}

[Landscape structure.]{.underline} Technological variation is not structured by position in the landscape. Across the `r n_localities` localities that yielded measurable Quina scrapers, no landscape variable accounts for an appreciable share of the variation in the six technological measures: assemblage size (*R*² = `r f(ls_size["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_size["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_size["p"])`), basin (*R*² = `r f(ls_basin["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_basin["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_basin["p"])`), distance to the nearest channel (*R*² = `r f(ls_dist["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_dist["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_dist["p"])`), and height above that channel (*R*² = `r f(ls_height["R2"], 3)`, pseudo-*F* = `r f(ls_height["F"], 3)`, *p* `r fp(ls_height["p"])`) (Table S12; the analysis frame itself is given in Table S11, and the localities are ordinated against each landscape variable in Fig. S6 and compared between basins in Fig. S8). These low *R*² indicate that landscape variables had little explanatory power for technological variation in Quina scrapers, provide no evidence for a structured spatial influence.

One weak pattern nevertheless runs in a direction worth noting. All six technological measures correlate positively with distance to the nearest channel (Spearman's ρ = `r f(min(ls_dist_rho), 2)`–`r f(max(ls_dist_rho), 2)`; @tbl-distance-correlations, and Fig. S7 for the scatter behind each coefficient), so that Quina scrapers from localities further from a channel tend to be thicker and more heavily reduced. The direction is the one predicted by work on the European Quina, where prolonged reduction are more pronounced at localities without ready access to abundant raw materials [@turq2000; @hiscock2009]. Two qualifications limit what can be made of this. No individual correlation reaches significance at this sample size, and the six measures are not independent of one another: edge angle covaries with GIUR, with the proportion of retouched edge and with the number of retouch generations (Section 5.1.1; @fig-edge-angle-reduction), so that the concordance of six coefficients does not amount to six independent confirmations. We therefore record the pattern as consistent with an established expectation, and as a hypothesis for landscape-scale work with larger samples, rather than as a demonstrated gradient.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-distance-correlations
#| tbl-cap: "Spearman rank correlation of each measure with distance to the nearest channel. The unit is the locality, not the specimen: each locality that yielded measurable Quina scrapers is represented by the median of those scrapers, and the count of localities is given in the text. The interval on ρ is a bootstrap percentile interval over localities; adjusted *p* is the Bonferroni adjustment across the six tests."

ls_fmt <- data.frame(
  Measure = unname(variable_labels[ls_dist_cor$variable]),
  rho = f(ls_dist_cor$rho, 2),
  ci  = sprintf("%s to %s", f(ls_dist_cor$lo, 2), f(ls_dist_cor$hi, 2)),
  p   = sub("^= ", "", vapply(ls_dist_cor$p, fp, character(1))),
  pbh = sub("^= ", "", vapply(ls_dist_cor$p_adj, fp, character(1))))
ls_fmt <- ls_fmt[order(-ls_dist_cor$rho), ]

knitr::kable(ls_fmt, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
             col.names = c("Measure", "ρ", "95% CI", "*p*", "Adjusted *p*"))
```

Across the study area, then, Quina scrapers were produced in essentially the same way, regardless of the basin in which a locality occurs, its elevation above the channel, its distance from water, or the size of the assemblage it has yielded: whatever governed the placement of these localities, it did not condition how the technology was practised at them.

# Discussion

The Quina material from these two basins is the product of a single technological concept, which we refer to as the Quina Valley. The primary evidence is the technological indistinguishability documented in Section 5.1; the raw material economy and the landscape invariance of Section 5.2 corroborate it. In technology, the scrapers display the diagnostic attributes of the Quina system: thick, asymmetric blanks with a back formed by cortex or by earlier removals; successive generations of retouch; the rhythmic alternation of convex and concave removals; and the continued production of resharpening flakes, some of which were used or reworked in turn. In raw material economy, the surface collections and the excavated assemblage at Longtan alike show a strong preference for trachyte, and that preference holds across the study area even though the gravel bars themselves vary significantly in composition from valley to valley. In their distribution across the landscape, neither technological characteristics nor raw material selection varies systematically with basin, height above the channel, distance to water or assemblage size. What the surface collections record, in other words, is not a scatter of superficially similar pieces but the repeated application of one way of working stone across a defined region.

Longtan is therefore no longer a single case. Its interpretation has been questioned by @Bourguignon2025QuinaChina and answered by @RuanEtAl2025. Part of that exchange rested on a misreading: the original report had left the origin of the Longtan Quina explicitly open, had itself doubted that the assemblage reflected European influence, on the grounds that dispersal should have left Quina systems across Central and South Asia where none has been reported, and had already advanced context-specific convergence as a plausible hypothesis [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a]. On the substantive points the reply set out the interdependence of flaking, retouch and ramification that makes the system techno-economic rather than typological; the flake thickness, asymmetry and cortex distribution that distinguish Quina blanks and cores from discoidal products; the proportion of grains accepted by the Bayesian OSL model, 60 to 83 per cent by sample; and the absence of size sorting, preferential orientation and appreciable inclination in Layer 3, consistent with *in situ* deposition.

The exchange nonetheless concerned what a single assemblage can be asked to carry, and it is on that point that the present study bears. Across several valleys and several terrace levels in two basins, assemblages appear that agree with Longtan in raw material selection, in blank selection, in the manner of retouch and in the degree to which tools were reduced. This recurrence is independent of the label: what the surface collections establish is that one techno-economic system, defined by the attributes measured above, was applied repeatedly across a defined region, and that finding holds whether or not its affinity with the European Quina is granted. With no independent age control (Section 4.1), what their recurrence establishes is distributional rather than chronological.

Quina-style artefacts are not confined to this region. Comparable material has been reported from Dahe in Fuyuan, Yunnan [@Ji2008], and Baicaoping in Liangshan, Sichuan [@ZhengEtAl2025Baicaoping], in southwestern China, and from Xinmiaozhuang in Yangyuan, Hebei [@WangEtAl2021XMZ1], in the north. Most of these assemblages have not been analysed technologically, and whether they represent the Quina system or Quina retouch alone remains open. They are best treated for the moment as leads rather than as established occurrences. The pattern documented here is of a different kind: within the Hengduan Mountains, the Quina system is a recurrent and identifiable regional entity, and the scattered reports elsewhere in China suggest that its distribution in East Asia may prove wider still.

Whether the same technology in two regions implies any connection between the hominins who made it is a question the evidence cannot settle, and the more productive line is to ask what problem the technology solved. In Europe that problem is reasonably well understood. Faunal assemblages from Quina sites are typically dominated by a single gregarious and migratory species, most often reindeer, although equids and bovids predominate in some regions [@delpechLenvironnementAnimalMousteriens1996; @delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011; @delpiano2022; @castelNeandertalSubsistenceStrategies2017]. The prey on which Quina groups depended were partitioned by topography rather than distributed evenly, reindeer occupying the ground between uplands and plain in a landscape of plateaux dissected by deep valleys, other species holding lower or more sheltered positions [@delpechLenvironnementAnimalMousteriens1996], so that movement was scheduled rather than opportunistic [@delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011]. Groups moving on such a schedule faced two problems at once: staying equipped while away from sources of stone, and not knowing in advance which tasks a given season and location would present. The three dimensions of the Quina system answer them in turn, in a reserve of volume that travels, an edge that can be restored without recourse to new stone, and a tool that can yield fresh edges of a different kind as needs change [@hiscock2009].

The setting on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau is not the European one, but it is likely to have posed a problem of the same structure. The regional monsoon record places the occupation of these basins at a climatic transition rather than within a settled phase. The nearest palaeoclimate records covering this period come from the lacustrine sediments of the Heqing Basin, about 60 km north of the Huangping and Binchuan basins and some 650 m higher, which are among the longest and most continuous environmental sequences available for the Asian monsoon domain and are highly sensitive to variation in the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) [@xiaoVariationSouthwestMonsoon2010; @zhishengGlacialInterglacialIndianSummer2011]. Magnetic and geochemical proxies there, on a chronology built from geomagnetic palaeointensity [@xuMagneticProxyHeqing2025], record a return to aridity between 69 and 57 ka, corresponding to MIS 4, and a generally humid MIS 3 thereafter, punctuated by repeated arid events [@yangIndianSummerMonsoon2025]. A diatom sequence from the same basin, dated by AMS ¹⁴C and magnetostratigraphy, resolves the interval of interest here directly: its zone spanning 64.8 to 49.8 ka brackets the MIS 4/MIS 3 boundary, opening with a deeper and cooler lake of low productivity and passing towards indicators of increasing runoff from the catchment, with the boundary itself placed at about 59 ka; the succeeding zone, from 49.8 ka, records shallow water and low runoff under a weakened monsoon [@liDiatomResponseClimatic2015]. Millennial-scale weakenings of the monsoon, each corresponding to a North Atlantic cold event, have been resolved in the basin for the past 52 ka [@houDifferentCoercivityMagnetic2026]; the earliest of them post-dates the interval dated at Longtan, and we cite this record to show that the monsoon of this region was liable to interruption of this kind rather than to date any interruption within the period of human presence. These records are treated here as regional context rather than as a proxy for conditions at the localities themselves, and for three reasons: the distance and altitudinal offset just noted; the reconfiguration of the Heqing lake's hydrology by tectonic uplift of the basin from about 132 ka; and the contribution to its water balance, during the interval in question, of meltwater from glaciers in the Yulong Mountains, where moraines have been dated to between 54 and 41 ka [@liDiatomResponseClimatic2015]. Read at that scale, what matters is not whether a particular stage was on balance wetter or drier, but that the occupation falls across the MIS 4/MIS 3 boundary, where an arid phase gave way to a strengthening monsoon in a system that the record of the following 40 kyr shows to have been liable to abrupt interruption.

Longtan provides the local counterpart to this regional picture, since it preserves both a robust chronology (Section 3) and a record of vegetation change. Pollen analysis of the terrace section at Longtan documents a shift from a pine–hemlock–grass assemblage to one in which arboreal pollen declines and herbs and wetland taxa rise, indicating a change from coniferous forest to a more open woodland-steppe; the Quina-bearing layer spans this transition [@ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a]. The spectrum is a mixture: wetland and herbaceous taxa record the immediate surroundings, while the montane conifers it contains, hemlock, spruce, fir and cedar, cannot have grown on a dry-hot valley floor and reach the site by the upslope and downslope air flows documented for the Hengduan Mountains [@zeng2025asian]. It is therefore read here as a relative shift towards more open conditions within the catchment rather than as a measure of the vegetation immediately around the site.

What can be said about the structure of such a landscape comes from its modern counterparts. Dry-hot valleys of the Jinsha drainage today carry the strongly seasonal, rain-shadowed climate described in Section 3, in which surface water is concentrated onto the valley floors, where groundwater draining from the flanking uplands sustains the rivers [@li2025investigating; @yangReviewResearchVegetation2016]; their vegetation is zoned by altitude, from savanna on the valley floors through transitional formations to forest on the surrounding heights [@jiangSeasonalDynamicsSoil2024]. It is the topographic partitioning rather than the particular vegetation that is likely to have persisted: whatever the detailed palaeo-configuration, water and forage in a valley system of this relief would have been distributed unevenly with respect to elevation rather than uniformly across the terrain.

Both landscapes were open, and in that respect the comparison is unremarkable: openness alone is compatible with many regimes of resource distribution, including some that place no premium on mobility. What the two settings share is more specific. In each, the resources on which hominins depended were organised seasonally and partitioned by relief, by the topographic separation of plateau, valley and plain in southwestern France [@delpechLenvironnementAnimalMousteriens1996] and by the altitudinal zonation of water and forage here. In southwestern France this structure is expressed in a settlement system of seasonally relocated camps with hunting and processing locations operating as satellites around them [@delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011]; for the Hengduan valleys no such inference can be drawn from surface material, and what the landscape indicates is only that resources of this distribution are more readily reached by moving through it than from a single fixed base. The difference lies in what produced that structure, glacial aridity in one case and monsoon seasonality in the other, and in the stone that was available to work; but the properties selected for are the same ones the European Quina is held to require, sizeable clasts of fine-grained rock [@delagnesShiftsNeandertalMobility2011], satisfied there by flint and here by trachyte.

A shared problem of this kind provides a mechanism for convergence, and would allow two regions with no contact between them to arrive at technological solutions that are functionally alike. The Quina Valley is on this reading a techno-economic adaptation to a landscape whose resources had to be reached by moving through it. Diffusion cannot be ruled out, however. Quina technology in the western Old World is closely associated with Neanderthals, and the boundaries of their range continue to be redrawn, so the question of origin is better left open at this stage than closed by the argument that is presently most economical.

One term in the argument is untested. In the European sequence it runs from prey structure through mobility to technology and rests on faunal assemblages; no fauna has been analysed from the Quina Valley, so the mobility to which the technology is here related is inferred from the landscape rather than observed in it. What would test the hypothesis is correspondingly clear: further excavation at Tianhuadong Cave [@hu2020Tianhuadong], and the recovery of primary-context assemblages in the Binchuan Basin, would supply the cores, the absolute ages and the faunal record that surface material cannot.

The Quina Valley also bears on a longer-standing question about the East Asian Middle Palaeolithic. The recent recognition of Levallois and Discoid technology in China has already made it difficult to hold that lithic technology there was lacking innovation before the Upper Palaeolithic [@huLithicTechnologiesGuanyindong2024; @ruanQuinaLithicTechnology2025a; @liEasternmostMiddlePaleolithic2018; @liTechnologicalBehaviorEarly2019], and the Quina system at Longtan added a further technology to the complex scenario. The present study shows that this is not an isolated occurrence but a way of working stone applied repeatedly across a region, and it offers a frame of reference for the assemblages elsewhere in China where Quina-like site has been reported but not yet analysed.

Two limitations qualify these results. Cores and flakes were not analysed and blank production is inferred from the attributes of the blanks themselves, so the first of the three dimensions rests on indirect evidence, while the other two are documented directly and in quantity. No local palaeoclimate record is available for the Binchuan Basin, and the regional setting is inferred from the Heqing sequence, which is treated throughout as context rather than as a local proxy.

# Conclusions

We have analysed the Quina scrapers and resharpening flakes collected from 27 localities in the Huangping and Binchuan basins, in the southern Hengduan Mountains, and asked two questions of them: whether they share a technological concept with the excavated material from Longtan, and, if they do, how the entity they define was organised across the landscape.

To the first question the evidence returns a consistent answer. In technology, the surface Quina scrapers cannot be distinguished from the Longtan material in the multivariate space of six technological variables, while those same variables separate both clearly from the non-Quina scrapers at that site; removing the specimens collected within the area of Longtan itself leaves the result unchanged. The uniformity of raw material selection and the absence of landscape structuring corroborate what the technology establishes. We have called this regional entity the Quina Valley. It establishes that Longtan is no longer a single case: one technological concept recurs across two basins, three valleys and several terrace levels, in a recurrence that is distributional rather than chronological; but that finding does not depend on whether their affinity with the European Quina is granted.

To the second question the answer lies in the raw material economy and its uniformity. Trachyte is not the most abundant lithology on the gravel bars, yet it accounts for almost all of the artefacts: Jacobs' index registers a strong selection of trachyte and an equally strong avoidance of sandstone, and that choice holds across the whole study area even though the composition of the bars differs significantly between valleys. What recommends trachyte is not how readily it could be had but what it is: its cobbles are larger, and its fine groundmass and low phenocryst content make it break predictably. In landscape position, technological variation is not structured by basin, by distance to the channel, by height above it, or by the size of the assemblage.

As to why so similar a way of working stone should appear in two regions this far apart, the most economical line of enquiry is to ask what problem it solved. In Europe, Quina is associated with resources that were seasonally organised and partitioned by topography, and with the mobility that such a distribution demands. The dry-hot valleys on the southeastern margin of the Tibetan Plateau are quite unlike that setting in climate, but not in the structure of the resources within them, which were seasonally organised and distributed by relief rather than evenly across the terrain. A shared problem of this kind supplies a mechanism for convergence. Diffusion cannot be ruled out, and the origin of this technology, together with the identity of the people who made it, is better left to further evidence than settled now.
